Literal Lock-In: How Test Language Shifts Literal Attraction
in Typed Decision Models on Bengali Idioms

Adib Sakhawat Email: adibsakhawat@iut-dhaka.eduhttps://github.com/sakhadib/literal-lock-insakhadib/literal-lock-inhttps://sakhadib.github.io/literal-lock-insakhadib.github.io/literal-lock-in    Syed Rifat RaiyanSystems and Software Lab (SSL)Department of Computer Science and EngineeringIslamic University of Technology, Dhaka, Bangladesh Email: rifatraiyan@iut-dhaka.eduhttps://github.com/sakhadib/literal-lock-insakhadib/literal-lock-inhttps://sakhadib.github.io/literal-lock-insakhadib.github.io/literal-lock-in
Abstract

Decision models, non-generative scorers that report a probability over caller-supplied options and emit no text, are increasingly deployed as routers, classifiers and guardrails. Because they generate nothing, rationales and chain-of-thought do not apply. We audit three: an encoder scorer, a decoder scorer and a closed API, entirely through interventions on their input, using expert-annotated Bengali idioms carrying a gold figurative and a gold literal gloss. Dropping an idiom’s own literal gloss into the option list draws every arm toward it, taking 65%65\% to 96%96\% of each arm’s remaining Bengali errors. A model ×\times language matrix over one shared item set shows how far this depends on the test language: every arm is 1.91.9 to 6.46.4 times more captured in Bengali than in English on the same paired entries, the commercial model’s apparent resistance is a property of its test language, and capability does not order the failure. Calibration degrades in all three arms, and on the open arms confidence inverts, so gating on it is worse than gating at random. On a semantics-free option list, where accuracy is at chance, the best-calibrated arm still reports mean confidence 0.820.82. Code and data are available at https://github.com/sakhadib/literal-lock-in.

†† ∗*Equal contribution.

1 Introduction

A decision model is given a question and a list of candidate options and returns a probability distribution over exactly those options. It does not sample and it produces no text. We call the interface typed because the caller declares the answer type and the option set in the request, and the response is guaranteed to be a distribution over exactly those options: the output cannot be malformed, only wrong. This class has grown quickly as infrastructure for routing, intent classification, content gating and tool selection, precisely because it is cheap, bounded and returns a number a caller can threshold on. An ecosystem analysis of 2,170 public projects finds it already embedded as a reusable decision component across domains (Ling et al., 2026), and proposals now place these models at the adjudication points of autonomous security harnesses (dos Santos Barbosa, 2026). The threshold is load-bearing.

That bounded interface is also an explainability problem. There is no rationale to inspect, no chain of thought to measure for faithfulness (Jacovi and Goldberg, 2020; Turpin et al., 2023), and in the commercial case no weights at all. What is left is the behavioral surface: the caller controls the question and the option list, and sees a probability vector. Any audit of this class has to be built out of that.

The obvious fallback, attributing the decision to input tokens (Ribeiro et al., 2016; Lundberg and Lee, 2017), is both unreliable here (Jain and Wallace, 2019; Adebayo et al., 2018; Hooker et al., 2019) and hard to read. How far an idiom’s parts map onto components of its figurative meaning varies by idiom and is not annotated in the corpus we use (Nunberg et al., 1994; Gibbs et al., 1989); for an expression at the non-decomposable end, a Shapley value over its words is computable but has no evident linguistic referent. We would rather intervene on the expression as a unit than report shares we cannot interpret (Appendix D).

We take the option set as the main intervention surface instead. Bengali bāgdhārā (idioms) are well suited to this because the expert resource we use ships, for each idiom, both a gold figurative meaning and a gold literal gloss: a ready-made, human-certified counterfactual distractor that no annotation effort of ours produced. Dropping that gloss into the option list turns a benchmark question into a targeted probe: does the model read the expression as an idiom, or as its words? Figure 1 shows one item answered both ways.

We contribute (i) a meaning-choice instrument for decision models in which the distractor family is the independent variable and the item, instruction and kk are held fixed, requiring no new annotation (§4); (ii) the Literal Attraction Rate, measured as a full model ×\times language matrix, which shows how far capture depends on the test language and that capability does not order it (§5.1); (iii) evidence that calibration degrades in all three arms, and that on the two open arms confidence becomes anti-diagnostic, with confidence-gated selective prediction worse than random gating (§5.2); (iv) a large dissociation in option-order dependence between the two scoring designs, with a methodological consequence for anyone evaluating this class (§5.4); and (v) a semantics-free control, run on all three arms and needing no annotation of any kind, bounding what each model reports when the options carry no information at all (§5.3).

2 Related Work

The decision-model class.

The evaluation literature is still forming, and reports quality somewhat below large models at far lower cost, with no independent accuracy advantage from the typed readout itself (Tang and Zheng, 2026; Rao and Callison-Burch, 2026; Ibrahim and Zaki, 2026; Guo et al., 2026; Yu and Yao, 2026). Two strands bear on ours. Ibrahim and Zaki (2026) report decision-model calibration exceeding most LLM baselines, and Li et al. (2026) build the confidence-gated cascade that follows from it; both depend on the returned confidence being diagnostic, and §5.2–§5.3 give conditions under which it is not. Concurrently Sun et al. (2026) find the decision follows an option’s name rather than its bound definition, and Xu (2026) flip 61.4% of correct decisions with short, fluent context additions chosen to redirect them. Appendix B sets out how each relates to our design.

Idioms in NLP.

Idiom resources and tasks are well established (Haagsma et al., 2020; Tayyar Madabushi et al., 2022; Chakrabarty et al., 2022), including for Bengali (Sakhawat et al., 2026), and the difficulty of figurative language for distributional models is long-noted (Shwartz and Dagan, 2019). Psycholinguistics frames the phenomenon as competition between a literal and a figurative route whose resolution depends on decomposability and context (Cacciari and Tabossi, 1988; Gibbs et al., 1989; Titone and Connine, 1999), and Oh et al. (2026) give mechanistic evidence that the competition is real inside a transformer: causal tracing recovers two pathways carrying the figurative and literal readings simultaneously, with early layers promoting the figurative one and a direct route keeping the literal one available.

Our d-lit intervention is the behavioral counterpart of that picture rather than a replication of it: they can ask how the literal route stays available inside a model they can open, we can only ask how often it wins in one that emits no text and, in one arm, exposes no weights (Appendix B).

Evaluating option scorers.

Option-order sensitivity and selection bias are documented for prompted generative LMs (Pezeshkpour and Hruschka, 2024; Wei et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2021). Sun et al. (2026) relay an independent evaluation harness reporting option-order sensitivity in Laya; that report is relayed rather than theirs, and we could not determine from it which checkpoint it covers, so we do not read it as establishing the behavior of the multilingual checkpoint we audit. What §5.4 adds is the comparison of option-marker against independent-option scoring over the full permutation set, and the caveat that permuting a list also relabels it, which that literature shows is itself a source of bias (Zheng et al., 2024).

Calibration and selective prediction.

Proper scoring and calibration measurement are standard (Brier, 1950; Gneiting and Raftery, 2007; Guo et al., 2017; Nixon et al., 2019; Kumar et al., 2019), as is the observation that calibration degrades under distribution shift (Ovadia et al., 2019; Jiang et al., 2021). Selective prediction gives the operational test (Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2019a; Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2019b; Traub et al., 2024). We report the combination that matters for deployment: accuracy decreasing with confidence, and a confidence gate underperforming a random one.

Behavioral testing.

Our design follows behavioral checklists, contrast sets and counterfactual minimal pairs (Ribeiro et al., 2020; Gardner et al., 2020; Kaushik et al., 2020; Naik et al., 2018; Jia and Liang, 2017); the contribution is carrying that tradition into a model class with no text output, where it is one of the few instruments left.

Low-resource evaluation.

Bengali has strong encoders and corpora (Bhattacharjee et al., 2022; Kakwani et al., 2020), and cross-lingual benchmarks establish the transfer gap (Hu et al., 2020; Ruder et al., 2021; Adelani et al., 2021); §5.7 localizes our failure to the Bengali side rather than to figurativeness.

3 Dataset

Source corpus.

We use Bangla Bagdhara (Sakhawat et al., 2026), a corpus of 10,361 Bengali idioms annotated under a 19-field schema by expert consensus.11 1 The published count is 10,361 and the distributed record file holds 10,359; the two missing rows are lost in the corpus’s own export rather than in our loader, which parses all 10,359 without error, so we cannot recover them. Of the 10,359, 8,876 carry every field the instrument requires. Each row carries the idiom, a gold figurative meaning in Bengali, an expert literal gloss, semantic tags, alternative surface forms certified as meaning-preserving, and a gold carrier sentence. We add no annotation; every intervention below is assembled from fields that already exist.

Its own benchmark on the same underlying task reports no model among 30 multilingual and instruction-tuned LLMs above 50% accuracy, against 83.4% for human annotators. Option construction differs, so those figures are not directly comparable to ours, but they locate the difficulty in the material rather than in our instrument.

4 Methodology

Figure 2 sets out the instrument end to end: what the corpus supplies, what each condition changes, and what comes back.

4.1 The meaning-choice task

Given an idiom, choose its gold figurative meaning from k=4k=4 candidates. Chance is 0.2500.250 throughout. The distractor family is the independent variable; the item, the instruction, kk, and per-item option-order randomization (seeded by item id and experiment) are held fixed across families, so a paired test across families compares one item under different option lists.

4.2 Distractor families and measures

The five families are d-rand (other idioms’ glosses at random), d-surf (glosses sharing surface tokens with the gold), d-sem (glosses from idioms sharing semantic tags), d-lit (one distractor replaced by the idiom’s own expert literal gloss) and d-hard (all three pressures at once). Appendix C gives each sampling rule, and Table 6 one complete item in the original script.

For the families containing a literal gloss, with ℓi\ell_{i} the literal option and gig_{i} the gold, the Literal Attraction Rate is

lar=1N∑i=1N[argmaxopi(o)=ℓi].\textsc{lar}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbf{1}\!\left[\arg\max_{o}p_{i}(o)=\ell_{i}\right].

lar is not 1−accuracy1-\text{accuracy}: it isolates the errors that are specifically a literal reading, and has no floor, since a model that never reads literally scores 00 while still being wrong.

4.3 Interventions and statistics

Seven interventions vary one thing each: the distractor family (E1), the idiom’s surface form (E2), the idiom as a unit (E3), the task language (E4), nothing (E5, derived from E1), the option text (E6) and the option order (E7). Appendices C and A give what each holds fixed and the typed question they share.

All intervals are 95% percentile bootstrap over items (2,000 resamples); paired comparisons use McNemar’s exact test; ECE uses 15 equal-width bins and AURC is reported against a random-gate baseline. The two open arms were built independently from a written contract, and on all 4,440 overlapping rows the gold key, gold position, idiom string and literal-distractor key agree at 1.0001.000, so every paired test is on identical questions (Appendix R).

4.4 Models

Three models span the design space (Table 4); none has an accompanying paper, so we identify them by their released artifacts.22 2 Laya-ml: convaiinnovations/laya, subfolder multilingual, on the Hugging Face Hub; the same repository ships the English-only checkpoint used as the control in §5.7. Lod-lille: mrn-dk/lod-lille-0.6B, same hub. Jev-1.13: typesafe/jev-1.13, served over OpenRouter’s /api/alpha/decisions endpoint, with no weights, training data or architecture published. Laya-ml is a bidirectional encoder scoring all options together from marker positions. Lod-lille is a decoder with independent-option scoring, each option attending only to the shared state, the question and itself from the same start position, which its model card reports as order-independent by construction in fp32; §5.4 finds that reordering and relabeling the list together still move its scores. Jev-1.13 is a closed commercial model behind a decisions API whose documentation names English as its primary and best-supported language; we know its interface and nothing else. Appendix A gives the call each one receives.

5 Analysis

5.1 Literal capture, and what it tracks

Table 1 gives the ladder for the two open arms on the 888 items they share; Figure 3 plots Laya-ml’s full set alongside (Appendices E, G). Lod-lille is the stronger model on every non-literal condition, by up to +0.133+0.133. Insert the idiom’s own literal gloss and the ordering reverses: Lod-lille falls to 0.0660.066, half of Laya-ml’s already-below-chance 0.1360.136, and the same holds for d-hard.

Within this pair, then, lar measures something accuracy does not: a model can be selected as “better” on a conventional benchmark while being worse at what that benchmark proxies for. Laya-ml and Lod-lille answer byte-identical questions in the same language, so the crossover between them is a paired result. The error is not diffuse: the decomposition under d-lit is gold / literal / other =0.136=0.136 / 0.6580.658 / 0.2060.206 for Laya-ml and 0.0660.066 / 0.8850.885 / 0.0480.048 for Lod-lille, both on those 888 items, and on the clearest of them Laya-ml places p=1.000p=1.000 on the literal gloss. Laya-ml’s full-set decomposition, 0.1510.151 / 0.6440.644 / 0.2050.205, is in Appendix E.

Capture tracks the language, not capability.

The arms above ran the literal condition in Bengali, while the commercial arm’s headline lar=0.047\textsc{lar}=0.047 is English, so the two are not comparable as they stand. We therefore ran the full model ×\times language matrix on the 3,265-item shared pool, every cell built by one function from one seed (Table 14, Figure 5); Jev-1.13’s English cell lands at 0.04720.0472 [0.0401,0.0545][0.0401,0.0545], matching its value in the English ladder of Appendix E.

Two things follow. First, every arm is far more captured in Bengali than in English on the same paired entries: 0.731→0.3790.731\rightarrow 0.379, 0.918→0.2410.918\rightarrow 0.241 and 0.304→0.0470.304\rightarrow 0.047, all paired McNemar p<10−100p<10^{-100}. Second, capture is not monotone in capability: Lod-lille, the stronger open arm on random distractors, is the more captured in Bengali, and Jev-1.13 the least. The open arms fall below chance here; Jev-1.13 does not, but loses 0.3900.390 of accuracy against its own English run. The pool is not neutral and its Bengali literal option carries a cue the English one lacks; on ladder items without it, Bengali capture is still 0.5810.581 and 0.8710.871 (Appendices I, J).

The capability ordering.

One scored condition is matched across all three arms, Bengali idiom with random distractors, and on it the commercial model is far ahead, 0.7360.736 against 0.3670.367 and 0.4840.484 (Appendix L). That is the ordering the calibration results below should be read against, and the one capture does not follow.

5.2 Confidence is anti-diagnostic

Table 2 gives the mean probability on the chosen option, split by outcome, on the literal-bearing families. Both open models are more confident when captured than when correct, Lod-lille extremely so (0.7870.787 against 0.4530.453), and their reliability curves slope downward under d-lit (Figure 4, Appendix F).

ECE depends on the binning (Nixon et al., 2019), so we also report the binning-free multiclass Brier score: 1.0301.030 and 1.3911.391 for the open arms under d-lit against 0.7500.750 for a uniform four-way distribution, so their reported probabilities are worse than declining to choose. Equal-mass bins move no ECE by more than 0.0110.011 (Appendix F).

Selective prediction therefore inverts on both open arms: restricting Laya-ml’s d-lit to its most confident 5% gives 0.0070.007 accuracy against 0.1510.151 at full coverage, and Lod-lille answers every item in its most confident 35% incorrectly (Appendix F). It is not an artifact of one confidence signal: Lod-lille’s separate confidence head, which estimates whether the answer is in the option list at all, shows the same inversion (0.6310.631 against 0.2950.295 over both literal-bearing families), and it survives AUGRC (Traub et al., 2024), which matters here because AURC aggregates risk conditioned on the accepted set and so over-weights failures made at high confidence, which is exactly where our inversion lives. For a random confidence signal AUGRC is half the error rate, so the baseline needs no simulation: under d-lit the open arms score 0.4480.448 and 0.4910.491 against 0.4250.425 and 0.4670.467, worse than random on that measure as on AURC.

Calibration degrades in all three arms; only the inversion is two-arm. Jev-1.13 looks well calibrated in English (ECE 0.0140.014, Brier 0.1070.107) and is not on the same items in Bengali (ECE 0.1350.135, Brier 0.6040.604), where its advantage over a random gate falls from 5.1×5.1\times to 1.4×1.4\times. It is not inverted, though, staying more confident when correct (0.7240.724) than when captured (0.6440.644), so the sign depends on the arm. This does not contradict Ibrahim and Zaki (2026): in-distribution calibration need not survive a targeted distractor shift, and it fails in the costly direction, since a confidence-gated cascade (Li et al., 2026) accepts without review exactly the tail where the open arms are least accurate (Appendix B).

5.3 Semantics-free control, on all three arms

The o4 ablation replaces every option’s text with a bare ordinal label, \bnঅর্থ 1–4 for the Bengali arms and meaning 1–4 for the commercial one, so the four options are distinguishable but carry no meaning. With the gold position randomized and no option carrying information, expected accuracy is 0.250.25 and whatever confidence survives above it is overconfidence, with no modeling assumption needed to read it. It needs no gloss and no literal annotation, so it is the one condition we can put to all three arms without the pool restriction; the commercial arm’s run is in English, so the labels differ in language from the other two while carrying the same absence of meaning (Figure 7).

The ordering reverses against Table 2. The best-calibrated model under real options is the worst when the options carry nothing: Jev-1.13 reports 0.8150.815 mean confidence at 0.2540.254 accuracy, an overconfidence of 0.5610.561, which we give as a gap rather than a binned ECE because the gap is a lower bound on ECE and needs no binning choice to defend. Lod-lille is the only one whose confidence falls close to the 0.250.25 a calibrated model would report (0.2820.282).

Jev-1.13 exposes a second field meant for exactly this case, a confidence that the answer is present in the option list at all, and it does not rescue the reading: on o4 it reports 0.7540.754 against 0.9460.946 with full glosses. The reference is not the 0.250.25 chance level of the top probability, since this field reports presence, so on a list where the answer provably is not present an informed value is near zero. The pattern matches Zhong et al. (2026) on a different task, with a scope condition that cuts both ways and that Appendix B sets out: a verification-typed call recovers what the choice type does not, and we have not tested whether that holds here. What the control shows is what a caller of this answer type is told, which is why we read it as the most portable finding: it needs no annotation and no matched language. McNemar between the two open arms under o4 is not significant (p=0.76p=0.76), so the instrument’s null behaves alike in both.

5.4 Option order is architecture-specific

We run every item under all 4!=244!=24 orderings of a fixed option set and record the chosen gloss’s identity, recovered as perm⁡[slot⁡(y^)]\mathrm{perm}[\mathrm{slot}(\hat{y})]; Appendix Q explains why the slot letter is the wrong unit for the answer.

One caveat applies to everything here. Permuting the list does two things at once: it moves each gloss and it changes which letter names it. They cannot be separated in this design, and the literature gives reason to think the second matters, since Sun et al. (2026) rebind option names to fixed definitions and find the decision follows the name, while Zheng et al. (2024) trace most selection bias in multiple choice to token-level priors on the option IDs. What we measure is therefore sensitivity to display order and labeling together, which is what a caller varies when they reorder a list, not a clean effect of position. Separating them needs a condition that moves each gloss while it keeps its own letter, which we did not run.

Table 21 gives six measures of that sensitivity, each on an item sample drawn separately per arm. The marker-based scorer changes its chosen gloss on 83.7%83.7\% of items against 10.7%10.7\% for the independent-option scorer and 13.3%13.3\% for the commercial one, a 7.8×7.8\times difference in the rate of answer changes and a 12×12\times difference in the within-item range of pp(gold). Each scoring design is represented by exactly one model, so the design cannot be separated from the backbone or the capability of the model carrying it; we read the pattern as consistent with the scoring architecture rather than as demonstrated to follow from it.

The invariance claim does not survive as stated.

Lod-lille is documented as order-independent by construction, each option being scored from the same start position so that no option sees another. Mapping every slot’s probability back to the option it displayed, a single option’s own score travels 4.0×10−24.0\times 10^{-2} at the median item and never stays below 10−410^{-4}, orders of magnitude above fp32 noise (Appendix Q). Given the caveat above we state the conclusion narrowly: a caller who permutes an option list does not get identical probabilities back. Whether the residue is positional or comes from the letters being reassigned we cannot say, and the second would be no less a failure of the guarantee than the first.

A slot preference follows, measured over all five families of the full ladder, where the gold position is randomized: Laya-ml takes slot B 37.2%37.2\% of the time against 14.6%14.6\% for slot A (Appendix Q). Here too slot and letter covary, so it is as consistent with a prior on the token B as with a preference for the second position. Either way, an evaluation of this class that fixes option order is partly measuring something other than the options. All results here randomize order per item, seeded by item id and experiment, and we would treat that as a default rather than a robustness check.

5.5 The option side is read lexically, and the idiom is not held as a unit

Two interventions probe how each side of the item is read, and both carry scope conditions we state with the result.

On the option side, scrambling the words inside every option costs almost nothing: writing signal for accuracy above chance as a fraction of the full-gloss condition’s, the three arms retain 0.9280.928, 0.9440.944 and 1.0051.005 of it. The companion truncation is weaker than it looks, since the median Bengali gloss is four words and truncation to six is a no-op on 77.8%77.8\% of options. The scramble is the result, and it converges with Sun et al. (2026) from the other direction; the scope condition is that the series runs on random distractors, where recognizing the right words already suffices, so it shows composition is not required here rather than that these models cannot compose (Appendix P).

On the idiom side, E3 perturbs the expression while holding the option list fixed. It covers only idioms of three words or more, so every manipulation changes the string on 99.7%99.7\% of items or better. Accuracy cannot carry the argument, because the condition is d-lit and the intact accuracies on E3’s own items, 0.1570.157 and 0.0720.072, already sit below chance. Agreement with the intact answer has no such floor, and that is where the claim rests: under word-shuffling the open arms return the same option on 0.7420.742 and 0.9170.917 of items, at least as often as under meaning-preserving rewrites (0.6570.657, 0.6770.677; Appendix N). The one manipulation that moves both is the gold carrier sentence, +0.080+0.080 and +0.117+0.117, so context rather than the idiom string carries the usable signal. That cuts both ways, since Xu (2026) flip 61.4% of correct decisions with short fluent additions chosen to redirect them (Appendix M).

5.6 What the item construction could explain

The literal gloss is an annotated field rather than a string we wrote, and in this corpus it is often lexically close to the idiom. Three properties could let a lexical matcher select it without reading anything. The idiom is a single word on 42.3%42.3\% of items, and on 18.0%18.0\% the literal gloss contains the idiom verbatim. In the matrix pool it is the only option written partly in Latin script, since no Bengali figurative gloss in the corpus contains a Latin character. And it is longer than the gold gloss on 67%67\% of items, though longest of all four on only 40.2%40.2\%.

Two of the three buy measurable capture (Table 3): verbatim overlap on both arms, and the Latin-script cue on Laya-ml, with Lod-lille’s interval covering zero. Length is the exception and needs separate handling, since the subset below does not remove it. Splitting on whether the literal option is the longest of the four moves lar by −0.034-0.034 [−0.055,−0.013][-0.055,-0.013] on Laya-ml and +0.020+0.020 [−0.024,+0.064][-0.024,+0.064] on Lod-lille, so Laya-ml is slightly less captured when it is: a real asymmetry in the material, not a route to capture.

Restricting to the 2,4802{,}480 items that are multiword, whose gloss does not contain the idiom and carries no parenthetical, removes both lexical cues and narrows the length gap to 36.636.6 against 32.432.4 characters. lar is still 0.5600.560 and 0.8910.891 against a chance level of 0.2500.250, and the length split stays null; Appendix J has the rest, including lar by idiom length.

5.7 Failure localizes to Bengali, in every arm

E4 asks the same question of an ordinary benchmark item rather than a literal-bearing one: hold the model fixed, swap the task language, keep the distractors random. Every arm moves by a large margin, Laya-ml +0.246+0.246, Lod-lille +0.380+0.380 and Jev-1.13 +0.230+0.230, each paired on that arm’s own shared items (all McNemar p<0.001p<0.001). Lod-lille reaches 0.8640.864 in English against 0.4840.484 in Bengali, so the figurative concepts appear largely available to it and the Bengali route is where the loss occurs, consistent with its documented English-only training evaluation. Laya-ml’s English-only checkpoint on Bengali script sits at 0.2830.283, barely above chance, against 0.3710.371 for the multilingual one on the same items, so the scorer does read Bengali where the checkpoint can. Here too the English condition presents the annotator’s nearest English idiom rather than a translation (Appendices K, J).

6 Discussion

Three cautions follow for anyone deploying this class. A returned probability is worth little without a measurement of what the model returns on a degenerate option list, a case that arrives from an upstream bug or an empty retrieval rather than from an adversary. A benchmark score is not by itself evidence against literal capture, since on our open arms the two move in opposite directions. And an evaluation that fixes option order is partly reporting position and labeling, which §5.4 shows cannot be separated here. None of this rebuts the cascade designs, whose cost and latency advantages are established (Tang and Zheng, 2026; Rao and Callison-Burch, 2026); it bounds them, since the property they rest on degrades first and silently.

7 Conclusion

Decision models are being placed at decision points, and the interface that makes them attractive is also what makes them hard to audit: no rationale, no chain of thought, and in the commercial case no weights. We have argued that the caller’s input is an adequate substitute, since every result here comes from changing the option list or the expression it asks about and reading the probability vector back, which needs no new annotation and works unchanged on a closed, text-free model.

One substituted option is enough. The idiom’s own expert literal gloss draws all three arms toward the literal reading, taking 65%65\% to 96%96\% of what each arm gets wrong in Bengali, and the model ×\times language matrix separates two explanations that are easy to conflate: capture falls by 0.260.26 to 0.680.68 in every arm when the paired entries are asked in English, so the commercial model’s apparent resistance belongs to its test language rather than to the model. Capability does not order the failure: the middle arm by accuracy is the most captured in Bengali. Nor is any of this visible to the caller: confidence inverts on the open arms under the literal shift, calibration degrades on all three, and on an option list stripped of semantics the arms still report between 0.280.28 and 0.820.82.

What the design cannot settle is set out in Limitations, and the cues that could have produced this result are measured in §5.6 rather than assumed away. We release the instrument and the per-item outputs.

Limitations

All three models are evaluated zero-shot, and this is the limitation we would weigh most heavily after the one below. Decision models are trained on a particular set of decision tasks, and the open arms’ own documentation reports that base checkpoints are weak on tasks outside that set. Some part of what we measure may therefore be out-of-distribution task transfer rather than literal capture specifically. The o4 control bounds this from one side, since it shows both open arms at chance accuracy with no detectable difference between them, and the d-rand to d-lit contrast is within-model and within-item, which removes any fixed task-transfer offset. Neither argument rules the confound out. A single lightly fine-tuned arm would settle it, and we have not run one.

Laya-ml’s run had its per-bucket temperatures unset, so its ECE figures are raw and we do not describe the arms as representing distinct calibration philosophies: both open arms are effectively untempered and comparable on that axis, and Jev-1.13’s internal calibration is unknown to us. Laya-ml also ran with bf16 requested on a Turing card, which has no bf16 tensor-core path, so the arithmetic falls back to fp32 CUDA cores (Appendix R); a reader reproducing on later hardware is not reproducing the same numerics.

Outside the capture matrix, which it ran on the full 3,2653{,}265-item pool, Lod-lille ran a fixed 10% subset (888 items), so its intervals there are roughly ±3\pm 3 points and its stratified cells are thin. Appendix O bounds the subset bias at 0.0160.016 and shows it changes no sign or ordering. E3 on the Lod-lille arm is 180 items and several of its perturbation contrasts are not individually significant. E7 covers 992 / 299 / 300 items rather than the full sets, drawn separately per arm, so its cross-arm comparison is unpaired.

Three of the interventions are weaker than their headings suggest, and we would rather say so than have it found. E7 cannot separate position from labeling, because permuting a list reassigns the letters with it; the condition that would separate them moves each gloss while it keeps its own letter, and we did not run it. E3 runs under d-lit, where intact accuracy is already below chance, so its accuracy rows have little room to fall and the conclusion rests on the intact-answer agreement instead; running it under d-rand would let accuracy carry the argument too. E6 runs under d-rand, where matching the right words is already enough to answer, so it shows composition is not required rather than that it is unavailable; the scramble under d-lit or d-sem is the test that would separate those, and it is unrun. None of the three affects §5.1, §5.2 or §5.3.

The matrix in §5.1 runs on the 3,265 items that carry a usable English literal gloss, which is not a neutral sample: for Laya-ml, in-pool lar is higher than out-of-pool while d-rand accuracy is unchanged, so the absolute rates there are higher than they would be corpus wide. That difference is not generic pool selection. Pool membership requires an English parenthetical inside the Bengali literal gloss, and Appendix J shows the parenthetical is itself worth +0.165+0.165 of lar on Laya-ml, which is most of the in-pool elevation. The language comparison is paired within item and within model, so the selection affects the levels rather than the direction. The matrix also covers the literal condition only; we did not run the other distractor families in both languages. The confidence results in §5.2 remain two-arm, because the commercial arm never shows the inversion, not because it was unmeasured: §5.2 reports its Bengali calibration from the matrix outputs.

The two language cells are also not symmetric in construction, and this is the limitation we would flag hardest. They are paired entries rather than identical items: the Bengali state is the idiom, while the English state is the annotator’s nearest English idiom rather than a translation of it. The two literal glosses are drawn from one annotated field in different ways, which leaves the Bengali literal option both lexically closer to its own state and, because it retains its English parenthetical, the only option in the list written partly in Latin script. Appendix J sets out all four asymmetries we could find and tests the two that recorded outputs can reach. Restricted to the 1,4291{,}429 items whose Bengali literal gloss shares no content word with the idiom, the capture gap is +0.358+0.358, +0.610+0.610 and +0.310+0.310 against headline gaps of +0.352+0.352, +0.677+0.677 and +0.256+0.256. Restricted to the ladder items whose literal gloss carries no English parenthetical at all, 5,4855{,}485 for Laya-ml and 560560 for Lod-lille, Bengali capture is still 0.5810.581 and 0.8710.871, against a chance level of 0.2500.250. Neither cue accounts for the result, though the second is worth a real +0.165+0.165 on one arm and we report it as such. What we cannot do without new runs is make the two cells symmetric by construction; a translation-paired corpus, or a Bengali cell with the parenthetical stripped, would settle what we can only bound.

More broadly, this is one corpus, one language, two small open models and one commercial endpoint. The semantics-free control is the only result here that we would expect to transfer as stated; the rest should be read as findings about these systems on this material, and as an instrument other people can point at theirs.

Distractors are drawn from the same corpus, so difficulty is corpus-relative rather than absolute. Jev-1.13 is a commercial endpoint and may change without notice; our results are a snapshot, and we report the exact call count and cost in Appendix R so the snapshot is at least auditable.

Ethics Statement

The corpus is a published, expert-annotated resource of idioms (Sakhawat et al., 2026); it contains no personal data and no content about identifiable individuals, and it is distributed under CC BY-SA 4.0. Our interventions rewrite option lists and perturb idiom strings, and produce no new annotation and no generated text.

The work audits two openly released models and one commercial API. We report failure modes in all three, including the vendor’s, and we have taken care to separate what is measured from what is inferred. Where a reading of our own data would have been more flattering than the data supports, we say so in the text: §5.1 states the pool selection effect against our cleanest number, and Appendix J reports a construction cue that accounts for part of the headline effect on one arm. Commercial endpoints are mutable, so the Jev-1.13 results should be read as a dated snapshot rather than a standing property of the product.

Bengali is under-served relative to its speaker population, and we think an audit that locates a failure in the language rather than in the task is the more useful kind to publish. The instrument, the per-item outputs and the analysis code are released under CC BY-SA 4.0, the corpus’s own license, and the two open checkpoints are used under the terms their model cards declare; Appendix R is the run record they correspond to.
