Appendix A The typed question

Every call in this paper sends one typed choice question and receives one probability vector. Nothing else is exchanged: there is no prompt template, no system message, no sampling parameter and no generated text. This is the whole interface, which is why every intervention in this paper acts on one of the two things the caller supplies: the state, or the option set.

Request.

For the commercial arm the body posted to /api/alpha/decisions is the following; the instruction string is the one in Table 5.

{
  "model": "typesafe/jev-1.13",
  "state": ¡idiom or carrier sentence¿,
  "questions": {
    "q": {
      "type": "choice",
      "instructions": ¡instruction string¿,
      "criteria": {
        "A": ¡gloss¿,
        "B": ¡gloss¿,
        "C": ¡gloss¿,
        "D": ¡gloss¿
      }
    }
  }
}

The two open arms are called locally with the same four fields: the idiom as state, the instruction string, and the four option texts keyed A–D. The option order is shuffled per item by a generator seeded with the item id and the experiment seed, so within an experiment the same item receives the same permutation in both open arms and in every family. The commercial arm’s blocks use their own seeds (Appendix R), so its permutations differ.

Response.

{
  "type": "choice",
  "choice": "B",
  "confidence": 0.75,
  "probabilities": {
    "A": 0.00,
    "B": 0.84,
    "C": 0.16,
    "D": 0.00
  }
}

We assert on every call that the returned keys are a subset of {A,B,C,D} and that the probabilities sum to 11 within 10−210^{-2}; no call in any run violated either.

Two confidence signals, and which one we use.

Note that confidence is not the maximum probability: in the example above it is 0.750.75 while maxo⁡p⁡(o)=0.84\max_{o}p(o)=0.84. It is a separate head whose documented job is to estimate whether the correct answer is present in the option list at all. Lod-lille ships the same arrangement. We log it as conf_head and report it where it matters (§5.2), but every cross-model number in this paper uses the maximum probability, because it is the only confidence signal all three arms define identically. Where the two disagree the head is not the more diagnostic of the pair: on Lod-lille’s captured items mean head confidence is 0.6310.631 against 0.2950.295 on correct ones, the same inversion the top probability shows.

Answer types we did not use.

The interface also accepts score (a bounded numeric judgment) and boolean questions. We use choice exclusively and deliberately. A score question would ask the model to rate a gloss in isolation, which destroys the property the instrument depends on: that the gold and the literal reading compete inside a single forward pass, exactly as the psycholinguistic account describes (Cacciari and Tabossi, 1988; Titone and Connine, 1999). A boolean question would do the same and additionally reintroduce a yes/no label whose name carries meaning of its own, which is the failure Sun et al. (2026) document. Keeping every experiment in one answer type also means the five distractor families differ in nothing but their option text.

Appendix B Positioning against concurrent work

The decision-model literature is a few weeks old at the time of writing, and several papers describe failures adjacent to ours. This appendix states what each one establishes, what it does not, and why our design is complementary rather than duplicative.

Mechanism versus behavior.

Oh et al. (2026) apply causal tracing to autoregressive transformers and recover two pathways carrying an idiom’s figurative and literal readings at once: early layers and specific attention heads promote the figurative interpretation while a direct route keeps the literal one available, and disambiguating context is integrated from the first layer onward. That is mechanistic evidence that the competition our d-lit condition exploits is real inside a model, and it is what makes our outcome measure interpretable rather than arbitrary: when a decision model places its mass on the literal gloss, there is a documented sense in which both readings were present and one won.

The two designs answer different questions, and the difference is the reason both are needed. Causal tracing requires weight access, token-level activations and a generative forward pass to intervene on. Two of our three arms release weights and the third does not, but none of the three emits a token stream to trace, and the commercial one is reachable only through an HTTP interface. Their method cannot be pointed at the systems that are currently being deployed as routers and guardrails; ours can, at the cost of saying nothing about where inside the model the competition is resolved. They establish how the literal route survives; we measure how often it takes over, in which language, and with what confidence attached.

Option names and option definitions.

Sun et al. (2026) hold a typed model’s option definitions fixed and permute which name is bound to which, and find decision-flip rates up to 70.4 points higher for semantically loaded labels than for neutral ones: the model follows the name rather than the definition it was given. They note that type-safety conceals this, because every output remains structurally valid.

Our o-series (§5.5) manipulates the complementary half. We hold the option names fixed at A–D and destroy the internal structure of the text bound to them, chiefly by shuffling words within each option (truncation is the weaker probe, Appendix P), and find accuracy almost unchanged. Read together, the two results point the same way from either side: within an option, these models are sensitive to lexical identity, and on random distractors their decisions do not depend on composed meaning. That falls short of showing they cannot compose, since composition is not needed on that condition (Appendix P). Neither result alone would establish that, because theirs is consistent with a model that reads definitions carefully but weights names more heavily, and ours is consistent with a model that reads definitions as unordered bags.

Context that flips decisions.

Xu (2026) append short, fluent, task-preserving context and redirect 61.4% of initially correct decisions, with targeted flip rates of 64.9–73.2% across systems. Our E3 carrier-sentence condition (§5.5) is the benign case of the same mechanism: embedding an idiom in its gold example sentence raises accuracy by 0.0800.080 and 0.1170.117 on the two open arms. The two findings are the same sensitivity with opposite signs, and the uncomfortable implication is that a caller cannot tell them apart from the interface. A model whose answer improves when helpful context is appended is, necessarily, a model whose answer moves when context is appended at all.

Rejection, and the answer type.

Zhong et al. (2026) report the failure closest to our o4 control: asked to choose among candidates that contain no correct answer, Jev rejects on about 7%7\% of cases, while selecting a correct candidate almost perfectly when one is present. Two scope conditions matter. Their items are paired arithmetic problems with an explicit rejection option, which ours are not, so the agreement is between a reading and a result rather than a replication. And they find the same model rejects correctly on about 99%99\% of those cases when asked instead for a Boolean verification of each candidate in turn. That is a different answer type from the choice type we hold fixed throughout (Appendix A), and it is a genuine possibility that a verification-typed call would recover what the choice type does not. Our claim is about what the choice interface reports, which is the interface these systems are deployed behind; it is not a claim that the underlying model cannot tell.

Calibration and cascades.

Ibrahim and Zaki (2026) evaluate decision models against 19 language models on 18 computational social science tasks, and report a median deficit of 11.6 F1 at 44 times lower cost, with confidence calibration exceeding most baselines; they recommend decision models as a cheap first stage that routes uncertain items onward. Li et al. (2026) build that system, accepting high-confidence verdicts and escalating the rest, and exceed a frontier model’s accuracy at 41% of its cost.

We reproduce the favorable calibration for the commercial arm on its own language (§5.2), so this is not a contradiction. The boundary we add has two parts. First, in-distribution calibration does not survive the shifts we apply: on the open arms it fails under a targeted distractor shift, and on the commercial arm, which stays calibrated under that shift in English, it fails under the change of language. On the open arms it fails in the direction that costs a cascade most: on the literal-bearing families the high-confidence tail is where the open arms are least accurate, so a confidence gate forwards exactly the items that should have been escalated. Second, and independent of any distribution assumption, the semantics-free control (§5.3) shows what each arm reports when the option list provably carries no information. A gate calibrated on real options has no defense against that case, and a degenerate option list is an ordinary consequence of an upstream bug or an empty retrieval.

What none of this settles.

All of the above, ours included, is zero-shot evaluation of base checkpoints. Tang and Zheng (2026) review 28 papers published within nine days of the first widely used release and conclude that the typed readout has shown no independent accuracy advantage, with the demonstrated gains in latency, cost and cascade placement. Whether any of these failure modes survives task-specific fine-tuning is, as far as we can determine, unmeasured by anyone so far.

Appendix C What each experiment changes

Table 7 states, for each experiment, the one thing that varies and the things held fixed. Reading down the “varies” column follows the argument: each row isolates one candidate explanation for the failure measured in E1.

E1, the ladder.

d-rand samples three other idioms’ figurative glosses uniformly. d-surf samples glosses sharing at least one surface token with the gold. d-sem samples glosses from idioms sharing at least one semantic tag. d-lit replaces one sampled distractor with the idiom’s own expert literal gloss. d-hard applies all three pressures at once. Duplicates are removed and the slate is topped up from the random pool if fewer than kk distinct options survive.

E3, perturbing the unit.

E3 runs on the literal-bearing option set, so its accuracies are comparable to d-lit rather than to d-rand: on the same 1,778 items Laya-ml scores 0.1760.176 under d-lit and 0.3530.353 under d-rand, against 0.1570.157 for the intact idiom here. The 0.1760.176 and 0.1570.157 are the same model on the same items under the same family, and they differ because E1 and E3 draw their random distractors from separate seed namespaces (1000 and 3000), so the two option lists share the literal gloss and the gold but not the two sampled distractors. Comparisons are therefore made within an experiment, never across one. v0 is the intact idiom. v1 shuffles its words, v2 reverses them, v3 deletes one word at random, v4 substitutes one word with a word sampled from another idiom, and v5 replaces the idiom with its gold carrier sentence. The option list is held byte-identical across all six, so the only difference reaching the model is the state string.

E6, ablating the options.

o0 is the full gloss. o1 truncates every option to its first six words. o2 shuffles the words within each option. o3 replaces each gloss with its counterpart in the other language. o4 replaces every option with a bare label carrying no semantics, which pins accuracy at chance by construction and is the control of §5.3.

Appendix D Why interventions on the option set

This appendix explains the design choice the rest of the paper rests on, for readers who want the reasoning rather than the result.

A decision model takes a question and a list of candidate options and returns a probability over exactly those options. It does not sample and it emits no text. Three of the usual explainability routes are therefore closed or compromised. There is no rationale to inspect and no chain of thought whose faithfulness could be measured (Jacovi and Goldberg, 2020; Turpin et al., 2023). Weights are available for two of our arms but not for the commercial one, so no method that requires opening every model, including probing and causal tracing, can be applied uniformly across the three (Oh et al., 2026). And input attribution, the usual fallback (Ribeiro et al., 2016; Lundberg and Lee, 2017), is not only unreliable here (Jain and Wallace, 2019; Adebayo et al., 2018; Hooker et al., 2019) but hard to interpret for this material.

The last point needs stating carefully, because it is what motivates everything else, and the standard shorthand for it is too strong. Idioms are not uniformly non-compositional. Nunberg et al. (1994) argue the opposite of the slogan usually attributed to them: idioms vary in how far their parts can be mapped onto components of the figurative reading, and many are idiomatically decomposable, with spill the beans distributing its meaning across spill and beans in a way that kick the bucket does not. Psycholinguistic work finds decomposability measurable and consequential for processing (Gibbs et al., 1989; Titone and Connine, 1999).

What follows is weaker than ill-posedness but enough for our purposes. A Shapley value over the tokens of an idiom is always computable, and for a non-decomposable expression there is no reason to expect the resulting per-token shares to correspond to anything linguistically real: the quantity is defined by the attribution game rather than by a decomposition the expression actually supports, and decomposability is a property of the individual idiom that we do not have annotated. The numbers will still arrive, and they will still read as an explanation. We therefore do not build on them, and intervene on the interface instead, which requires no assumption about where an idiom’s meaning sits.

What remains is the interface itself. The caller controls the question and the option list and observes a probability vector. So we intervene there. The corpus supplies, for every idiom, both a gold figurative gloss and an expert literal gloss, which means a counterfactual distractor is already annotated and we create no new labels: dropping the literal gloss into the option list turns a benchmark item into a targeted probe of whether the expression was read as an idiom or as its words. Holding the item, the instruction and kk fixed while varying only the distractor family makes the comparison within-item and within-model, so a difference between two families cannot be explained by item difficulty, by the prompt, or by anything about the model that does not change between the two calls.

The same logic produces the other five interventions; E5 is an analysis of E1’s outputs rather than an intervention. If the failure were about the idiom’s surface form rather than its meaning, E2 would show it (Appendix N). If the model held the expression as a stored unit, breaking the unit in E3 would hurt. If the problem were figurativeness rather than the language, E4 would not move. If the model read options as sentences rather than as bags of words, E6 would collapse under scrambling. If the scorer were order-independent as documented, E7 would return the same gloss under all 24 permutations. Each experiment is an attempt to explain the E1 result away, and the paper reports which attempts succeed.

Appendix E The full distractor ladder

Table 8 gives every family for every arm. Two caveats on the commercial column: its numbers are English, and its d-surf and d-sem rows run on the larger 8,761-item English pool rather than the 3,265-item literal pool, because those families need no literal gloss.

What the ladder is for.

The five families form an ordered difficulty scale in which only the distractor construction changes. d-rand draws three other idioms’ figurative glosses uniformly, so a wrong answer requires confusing two unrelated meanings. d-surf draws glosses belonging to idioms that share a word with the target, which makes the distractors lexically adjacent to the state but not to the gold. d-sem draws from idioms sharing a topical tag, which makes them semantically adjacent to the gold. d-lit replaces one distractor with the target’s own expert literal gloss. d-hard combines the literal gloss with one surface and one semantic neighbor. Reading down the first four rows therefore separates three different kinds of hardness, and the point of the ladder is that they are not interchangeable.

The literal family is not merely the hardest.

Measured as a drop from d-rand, the lexical and semantic neighbors cost Laya-ml 0.0290.029 and 0.0340.034, and Lod-lille 0.0720.072 and 0.0380.038. The literal gloss costs them 0.2160.216 and 0.4180.418: roughly six to eleven times as much as either neighbor family, from a single substituted option. A benchmark that stopped at d-sem, which is where most distractor-hardness work stops, would have recorded these two models as moderately sensitive to distractor difficulty and would have missed the effect entirely. That is the argument for the family being the independent variable rather than a robustness check.

The commercial column does something different.

Jev-1.13’s ordering is not the same shape. Its worst family in English is d-sem at 0.8290.829, and the literal family at 0.9310.931 is easier for it than the semantic one, which inverts the open arms’ ordering. Those two rows come from different pools, so that comparison is indicative; the paired version is on the 3,2653{,}265 items both d-rand and d-lit share, where the literal gloss costs it only 0.0370.037 (0.9680.968 to 0.9310.931) against 0.2160.216 and 0.4180.418 on the open arms. Read alone, that looks like a model which has simply solved the literal distractor. Read against the Bengali column of Table 14, where the same model on the same construction is captured at 0.3040.304, it reads instead as a model for which the literal distractor is easy in English. Only the matrix distinguishes the two, which is why we report the English ladder and the matrix together rather than either alone.

Why d-hard adds little.

d-hard keeps d-lit’s literal gloss and replaces its two random distractors with harder neighbors, yet costs only a further 0.0070.007 and 0.0030.003 on the open arms. Once the literal gloss is present it absorbs essentially all of the available error: the remaining two slots could be filled with anything without changing the outcome much. This is also why we report lar on both families and treat d-lit as the headline, since it is the cleaner single-variable manipulation.

Appendix F Selective prediction in detail

Selective prediction asks what happens if the caller answers only the items the model is most confident about. A useful confidence signal makes accuracy rise as coverage falls. Table 9 reports accuracy at low coverage for the two open arms, on the random-distractor condition and on the literal-bearing one.

This is the result with the most direct operational consequence. A cascade that forwards high-confidence answers and escalates the rest (Li et al., 2026; Ibrahim and Zaki, 2026) forwards precisely the items on which these models are wrong, and escalates the ones they would have got right.

How to read the table.

Each row fixes a coverage level and reports accuracy on the retained items, so a row is not a subset of the row above it in any model-independent way: the items retained at 0.050.05 coverage are whichever items that model ranked highest, which differ between the two arms and between the two families. The comparison the table supports is therefore vertical within a column, not horizontal across them. The quantity to watch is the sign of the gradient. In the two d-rand columns it is the sign a caller expects, with one small reversal at the top of Lod-lille’s (0.9770.977 at 5%5\%, 0.9890.989 at 10%10\%), and the magnitude is substantial: Lod-lille reaches 0.9770.977 in its most confident twentieth against 0.4840.484 at full coverage. In the two d-lit columns it is reversed, and the reversal is monotone rather than noisy, which is what makes it an inversion of the mechanism rather than a weak signal. The four zeros in the last column are literal: across the 311311 items making up Lod-lille’s most confident 35%35\% under d-lit, the model is correct on none.

Calibration without binning.

Table 10 reports the same distributions under three metrics. The point of giving three is that each fails differently. ECE with equal-width bins is the field standard and is also the metric Nixon et al. (2019) show to be sensitive to the binning: with 15 equal-width bins most of the mass can land in one or two bins, and an estimator averaging over near-empty bins can move with the bin count. Replacing them with 15 equal-mass bins, which is their adaptive variant, changes nothing material here: the largest shift across the nine cells is 0.0110.011, and the ordering of the arms is identical. So the calibration failure is a property of the distributions, not of our bin edges.

The Brier score is the stronger statement because it needs no bins at all. It is strictly proper, so no reporting strategy beats reporting one’s true beliefs, and it has a fixed reference point: a model that returns 0.250.25 on all four options scores exactly 0.7500.750. Under d-rand both open arms sit below that reference, which is what a model carrying some signal should do. Under d-lit both rise above it, to 1.0301.030 and 1.3911.391. This is worth stating plainly because it is stronger than miscalibration: on the literal-bearing condition, a caller integrating these models’ full reported distributions is worse off than a caller who replaced them with a flat prior. Jev-1.13 in English stays far below the reference throughout, and the one cell where it approaches a visible calibration cost is d-hard (0.2200.220, ECE 0.0470.047), which with d-lit is one of the two conditions containing the literal gloss.

Appendix G Stratified results

Literal capture is not concentrated in rare or obscure idioms, which would be the comfortable explanation. Splitting Laya-ml’s d-lit condition by the corpus’s own frequency annotation gives lar 0.6710.671 on very common idioms (n=1,146n=1{,}146), 0.6460.646 on common (n=6,200n=6{,}200), 0.6150.615 on rare (n=1,507n=1{,}507) and 0.5650.565 on very rare (n=23n=23). If anything the effect is strongest on the most familiar expressions, which is the opposite of a long-tail story and consistent with these being the idioms whose literal readings are most available.

The gradient is monotone across the three populated strata and spans 0.0560.056, which is small against the effect itself but points the wrong way for a familiarity account. We would not build on the very rare cell: at n=23n=23 its interval is wide enough to be consistent with anything, and we report it only so the stratification is complete.

The corpus’s cultural_significance field is unusable as a stratifier: 10,337 of 10,359 rows carry the same value. We mention this because it is the field a reader would most want stratified, and its absence is a property of the resource rather than a choice of ours.

Appendix H Output distributions

The three arms do not merely differ in accuracy; they place their probability mass very differently, and the shape of that mass is what makes the confidence results of §5.2 possible. Table 12 summarizes the returned vectors.

That last point is worth stating separately, because it is the mechanism behind the inverted reliability curves. A model that found the literal option merely distracting would spread mass and lose accuracy together. Both open arms do the opposite: adding the literal gloss concentrates the distribution onto it. On 21 items Laya-ml returns p=1.000p=1.000 on the literal gloss and p=0.000p=0.000 on the gold, to three decimal places.

How to read the entropy column.

Normalized entropy is the entropy of the returned four-way vector divided by log⁡4\log 4, so 11 is uniform and 00 is a point mass. It is reported alongside the maximum because the two can move independently and the pair identifies the shape. A model that is uncertain between two options and has ruled out the other two has a high maximum and a middling entropy; a model hedging across all four has a low maximum and a high entropy. Both open arms under d-rand sit near 0.890.89, which is a mild preference over an almost flat vector: at 0.440.44 mean maximum they are closer to guessing than their accuracy suggests. Under d-lit Lod-lille’s entropy falls to 0.4970.497 while its accuracy falls to 0.0660.066, so it moves from hedging to committing at precisely the point where committing is wrong.

Jev-1.13 is a different instrument. Its entropy is 0.0680.068 under d-rand and 85.2%85.2\% of its answers exceed 0.950.95, so it is nearly a hard classifier that happens to expose probabilities. That matters for how its calibration figures should be read: a model returning 1.0001.000 almost always has little room to be miscalibrated in the ECE sense while it is accurate, and correspondingly no room to signal doubt when it is not. Its low ECE in Table 2 and its 0.8150.815 confidence on the semantics-free control (§5.3) are the same property seen from two sides.

Worked examples.

Table 13 gives five items in the original script with the annotators’ own glosses and English equivalents. They are drawn from the extreme tail rather than sampled, items where the mass on the literal gloss is at or near 1.0001.000, and we flag the selection because the tail is what an aggregate lar of 0.6440.644 does not convey. All five also come from the 2,4802{,}480 items of §5.6 on which neither lexical cue is available, so none of them is a case where the idiom and its literal gloss are the same string or where the literal option is the only one in Latin script. What they add is the kind of expression involved: \bnজলের দাম (joler dam), the price of water, means dirt cheap, and \bnদু কথা (du kotha), two words, means a trifling remark. These are everyday constructions, and the literal reading the model selects is in every case the annotators’ own rather than one we wrote.

Appendix I The capture matrix

Table 14 gives the six cells of §5.1 with the accuracy column alongside lar; Table 15 gives the bootstrap intervals on those lar values and the paired within-model language effect. All cells are n=3,265n=3{,}265 and were built by one function from seed 21000. The language effect is positive on every arm and the intervals on the two language cells are disjoint in every case. Jev-1.13’s English lar here agrees with its English-ladder value to four decimal places, 0.04720.0472, which is why we treat the two constructions as measuring the same thing. Its accuracy in that cell is 0.9260.926 against 0.9310.931 in Table 8: same model, same items, same family, but the two runs draw their two sampled distractors from different seed namespaces (12000 and 21000), so the option lists share the gold and the literal gloss and differ in the rest. Capture is insensitive to that and accuracy is mildly sensitive, which is what one would expect.

Why this table is the one we defend hardest.

Everywhere else in the paper a comparison moves one thing and holds the rest fixed within one arm. Here the design is a full crossing, so the same 3,2653{,}265 items, the same distractor draw and the same seed produce all six cells, and both margins are readable. The language margin is large and uniform in sign: every arm is more captured in Bengali, by +0.352+0.352, +0.677+0.677 and +0.256+0.256. The capability margin is not even monotone. Lod-lille, which beats Laya-ml by +0.133+0.133 on random distractors over the 888 items they share (Table 1), is the most captured arm in Bengali, and the strongest arm is the least captured in both languages. A single ordering of these three models therefore cannot predict their capture, while knowing the test language can.

Reading accuracy against lar.

The two columns per language are not redundant. Accuracy counts items answered correctly; lar counts items where the chosen option was specifically the idiom’s own literal gloss, which is one of the three available errors. The gap between them is the residual error on other distractors. For Lod-lille in Bengali, accuracy 0.0440.044 and lar 0.9180.918 leave 0.0380.038 for everything else, so the literal gloss accounts for almost the whole error budget rather than merely enlarging it. For Jev-1.13 in Bengali, accuracy 0.5360.536 and lar 0.3040.304 leave 0.1600.160, so even its errors are less literal-dominated. This is the sense in which capture is a specific failure and not a restatement of accuracy.

What the table cannot settle.

Three things. The pool is the 36.8%36.8\% of the corpus that carries a usable English gloss, so the levels are pool levels (Appendix J). The two language cells are paired entries rather than translations, and are asymmetric in construction in four ways we enumerate in the same appendix. And the matrix covers the literal condition only; we did not cross the other four families with language, so we cannot say whether the language effect is specific to literal capture or general to distractor difficulty. The first of these affects levels, the second we test in part, since the recorded outputs reach two of the four asymmetries, and the third is simply unrun.

Appendix J How the two language cells were built

The capture matrix is the result we lean on hardest, so this appendix states exactly how its two language cells were constructed, lists every asymmetry between them that we could find, and reports the tests of the two that the existing outputs can reach.

Where the glosses come from.

Neither literal gloss is a translation produced by us or by a machine. The corpus annotates one field per idiom, literal_meaning, written in Bengali with an English parenthetical alongside it, so a single expert-authored field carries both readings. The Bengali cell uses that field as written. The English cell uses the parenthetical alone, recovered by a regular expression that accepts a parenthesized span only if it contains at least three ASCII letters and is at least 60%60\% ASCII alphabetic, which excludes Bengali asides and bare numerals. Of 8,8768{,}876 items, 3,3913{,}391 carry such a parenthetical, 3,3523{,}352 of those also carry an English equivalent idiom, and 3,2653{,}265 survive a final cut requiring the English literal gloss to be lexically distinct from the English gold gloss (Jaccard <0.34<0.34). That pool of 3,2653{,}265 is the matrix. The provenance matters because a machine-translated English gloss would make the English cell a measurement of the translator; an annotator-written one does not.

The four asymmetries.

We can state these precisely, which is better than asserting the cells are matched.

(i) The state differs in kind. The Bengali state is the idiom itself. The English state is the annotator’s nearest English idiom, taken from the similar_in_english field, not a translation of the Bengali one. The cells are therefore paired entries, and we use that phrase in the paper rather than “identical items”.

(ii) The Bengali literal option is bilingual. Because the Bengali cell uses the annotated field as written, and pool membership requires that field to contain an English parenthetical, every one of the 3,2653{,}265 Bengali literal options contains its own English gloss inside it, averaging 4444 characters against 2424 for the English literal option. This is the most direct of the four, because it supplies a cue that has nothing to do with reading the expression: no Bengali figurative gloss in the corpus contains any Latin character, so whenever the literal option carries a parenthetical it is the only option in the list written partly in Latin script. It is also usually the longer of the two glosses, though not reliably the longest of the four: that holds on 40.2%40.2\% of items, and §5.6 shows length does not predict capture. “Select the option containing English” would reproduce the Bengali capture numbers for all three arms and would also predict the English cell showing less capture, because there the cue is absent. We test it below.

(iii) The distinctness cut applies to one side only. The Jaccard <0.34<0.34 filter between gold and literal gloss was applied in English and not in Bengali. Measured after the fact, the filter turns out not to bind: mean gold-versus-literal Jaccard is 0.0290.029 in Bengali against 0.0520.052 in English, so the Bengali side is the more separated of the two and would have passed the cut almost everywhere. This asymmetry is procedural rather than consequential.

(iv) The literal gloss echoes the state more often in Bengali. With (ii), this is one of the two that could plausibly manufacture the result. The Bengali literal gloss shares at least one content word with the Bengali idiom on 56.2%56.2\% of pool items; the English literal gloss shares one with the English equivalent idiom on 25.1%25.1\%. A model doing order-free lexical matching on the option side, which §5.5 shows all three partly are, has a surface hook into the Bengali literal option that it lacks in English.

Testing asymmetry (iv).

The existing per-item outputs are enough to test it without running anything new. Split the pool on whether the Bengali literal gloss shares a content word with the idiom and read lar in each stratum (Table 16, upper block). If the hook were driving capture, the overlap stratum would be far more captured in every arm. It is not: the effect is +0.026+0.026 for Laya-ml, +0.130+0.130 for Lod-lille and −0.129-0.129 for Jev-1.13. The sign is not even consistent across arms, and on the commercial arm the hook is associated with less capture, which is the opposite of the predicted direction.

The sharper test restricts both language cells to the 1,4291{,}429 items where the hook is absent and re-reads the gap there (lower block). It barely moves: +0.358+0.358, +0.610+0.610 and +0.310+0.310, against headline gaps of +0.352+0.352, +0.677+0.677 and +0.256+0.256. For two of the three arms the gap is slightly larger once the hook is removed. We read this as showing that asymmetry (iv) does not account for the Bengali–English difference, not as showing the cells are equivalent; a corpus paired by translation rather than by annotator judgment would settle what we can only bound here.

Testing asymmetry (ii).

The capture matrix cannot test this, because every item in its pool carries a parenthetical by construction. The Bengali arm of E1 can. It runs the d-lit family over all 8,8768{,}876 items, and on 5,4855{,}485 of them the literal gloss carries no parenthetical at all, so the Latin-script cue is simply absent. If the cue were what produces capture, those items should show little of it.

They show a great deal of it (Table 17). Two things follow, and they point in opposite directions.

First, the mechanism is real, at least on the marker-based scorer. Laya-ml’s lar is 0.7460.746 where the cue is present against 0.5810.581 where it is absent, a difference of +0.165+0.165 with a bootstrap interval of [+0.145,+0.184][+0.145,+0.184]; on Lod-lille it is +0.037+0.037 with an interval straddling zero. Part of the Bengali capture we report is therefore attributable to a cue rather than to a reading of the expression, and we would not have found that without looking.

Second, it is not what produces the result. With the cue entirely absent, Laya-ml still selects the literal gloss on 58.1%58.1\% of items and Lod-lille on 87.1%87.1\%, against a chance level of 0.2500.250 and against English-cell capture of 0.3790.379 and 0.2410.241. The effect is also specific: on the three families that contain no literal option, the same split moves accuracy by at most 0.0420.042 with inconsistent sign, so the parenthetical stratum is not simply the easier or harder half of the corpus.

This bounds the cue rather than removing it. It covers the two open arms and not the commercial one, and the no-cue stratum is a different item set from the pool, so these numbers are not a clean subtraction from the matrix. The experiment that would settle it is to strip the parenthetical from the Bengali literal option and re-run the Bengali cell, which we have not done.

Item construction, and what it could explain.

The literal gloss is an annotated field rather than a string we wrote, and in this corpus it is often lexically close to the idiom. Of 8,8768{,}876 items, 3,7523{,}752 (42.3%42.3\%) have a single-word idiom, 3,3333{,}333 have two words and the rest three or more. On 1,3031{,}303 items (14.7%14.7\%) the Bengali part of the literal gloss is identical to the idiom, and on 1,5991{,}599 (18.0%18.0\%) it contains the idiom string verbatim. The literal option averages 41.141.1 characters against 31.731.7 for the gold gloss and is the longer of the two on 67%67\% of items, although against all three alternatives it is the longest on only 40.2%40.2\%. Some entries are also better described as polysemous words than as idioms: for \bnচারপায়া (charpaya), “four-legged” and “rope cot” are two senses of one word rather than a literal and a figurative reading of a phrase. We did not filter these out, because the corpus’s own annotation is what defines the literal and figurative options and we did not want to substitute our judgment for it, but a reader should know they are in the pool.

lar by idiom length is not what a string-matching account predicts. For Laya-ml it runs 0.6350.635, 0.6840.684, 0.5950.595 and 0.5730.573 across one-, two-, three- and four-or-more-word idioms, peaking in the middle rather than on the single-word items where the idiom and its gloss are most often the same string. Verbatim overlap does matter: lar is 0.7670.767 where the gloss contains the idiom against 0.6160.616 where it does not (+0.151+0.151, bootstrap [+0.128,+0.175][+0.128,+0.175]), and 0.9860.986 against 0.8660.866 on Lod-lille (+0.120+0.120, [+0.089,+0.150][+0.089,+0.150]). Removing both lexical cues at once, which leaves the 2,4802{,}480 items that are multiword, carry no verbatim overlap and carry no English parenthetical, leaves lar at 0.5600.560 and 0.8910.891 and accuracy at 0.1870.187 and 0.0790.079 (Table 3).

Length is not removed by that subset, so we test it on its own. Reconstructing each d-lit option list under the run’s own seed, the literal option is the longest of the four on 40.2%40.2\% of all items and averages 41.141.1 characters against 31.531.5 for the other three. Inside the cue-free subset both gaps narrow, to 30.6%30.6\% and 36.636.6 against 32.432.4 characters, so the subset does attenuate length without eliminating it. It does not need to: splitting on whether the literal option is the longest gives lar 0.6230.623 against 0.6570.657 on Laya-ml, a difference of −0.034-0.034 [−0.055,−0.013][-0.055,-0.013] in the opposite direction to the cue, and 0.8970.897 against 0.8770.877 on Lod-lille, +0.020+0.020 [−0.024,+0.064][-0.024,+0.064]. Within the cue-free subset the two differences are −0.026-0.026 [−0.069,+0.016][-0.069,+0.016] and +0.056+0.056 [−0.025,+0.130][-0.025,+0.130], neither distinguishable from zero. Length is a genuine asymmetry in the material and not a route to capture, which is why we report it separately rather than claiming the subset removes it. The worked examples in Table 13 are drawn from this subset so that none of them rests on verbatim overlap or the Latin-script cue. All five do share a content word with their literal gloss, which is asymmetry (iv), and Table 16 shows that overlap does not carry capture.

What this appendix does not establish.

Asymmetry (i) remains untested: we cannot ask what the arms would do on an English state that is a literal translation rather than an idiomatic equivalent without running that condition. We flag it in Limitations rather than dismissing it.

Appendix K Cross-lingual arms

Figure 6 plots the E4 conditions discussed in §5.7. E4 differs from the capture matrix in two ways that are easy to conflate, so we state them. E4 uses the d-rand family, with no literal gloss anywhere in the option list, and it asks what the language costs on an ordinary benchmark item. The matrix uses d-lit and asks what the language does to literal capture specifically. The two therefore measure different things and the figure should not be read as a version of Table 14.

What the four Laya-ml bars are.

Laya-ml has two checkpoints in play. The first two bars are the multilingual checkpoint on Bengali and on English, which is the within-model language contrast. The third and fourth use the vendor’s English-only checkpoint, and exist as a control rather than as a result: the third runs it on the English condition, where it should and does perform, and the fourth runs it on Bengali script, where it sits at 0.2830.283, barely above the 0.2500.250 chance line. That fourth bar does one specific job. A checkpoint documented as unable to read the script fails here in the documented way, while the multilingual checkpoint on the same items reaches 0.3710.371, so the scoring harness does pass Bengali through to a model that can read it. What the bar cannot do is rule out a harness that depresses Bengali scores without erasing them, since an English-only checkpoint would fail on Bengali either way; it shows the harness is not erasing the language, not that the harness contributes nothing to the deficit.

The gains are not uniform, and the ordering is informative.

Lod-lille gains the most (+0.380+0.380), Laya-ml and Jev-1.13 roughly similar amounts (+0.246+0.246 and +0.230+0.230). Lod-lille is the arm whose documentation states English-only training evaluation, and it is also the arm whose Bengali accuracy (0.4840.484) is closest to chance relative to its English accuracy (0.8640.864). The natural reading is that its figurative knowledge is largely intact and the Bengali interface is where it is lost. We cannot confirm that without probing the model, which we do not do here, and we note the alternative: a model may also be worse at Bengali figurative semantics specifically, which would produce the same external behavior.

Why the error bars matter here.

The three arms run at very different nn, so the intervals differ by a factor of three in width. Lod-lille’s English condition in particular runs on its 10%10\% subset. All three gaps clear McNemar at p<0.001p<0.001 on paired items, which is the test to read rather than the overlap of the bars, since the bars are unpaired marginals and a paired effect can be significant while marginal intervals overlap.

Appendix L The matched three-way condition

Figure 8 plots Table 18, the one condition that is matched across all three arms: Bengali idiom, Bengali glosses, random distractors, four options, gold position randomized, one instruction string. The sampled distractors are not the same three, because the commercial arm’s blocks ran under their own seed namespace (Appendix R); what is held is the construction, not the byte string.

Why only one condition qualifies.

Every other comparison in the paper is scoped by something the three arms do not share. The literal condition needs an annotated literal gloss, which exists in Bengali for the whole corpus but in English only for the 3,2653{,}265-item pool. The confidence results need a comparable confidence signal; the maximum probability is the only one all three define identically (Appendix A), and it is uncalibrated on Laya-ml, whose shipped per-bucket temperatures were not applied (Appendix R). Beyond it the arms expose different auxiliary signals, Lod-lille’s separate confidence head and Jev-1.13’s presence-of-answer field, which we report where they bear on a result (§5.2, §5.3). The order experiment needs the full permutation set, which we ran at different nn per arm. This condition needs none of that, so it is the one place where a bare capability ordering can be read without a caveat attached.

What the ordering is for.

It exists to be contradicted later. The ordering is Jev-1.13 0.7360.736, Lod-lille 0.4840.484, Laya-ml 0.3670.367, with every pairwise McNemar significant at p<10−9p<10^{-9}, so it is not a close call. Three later results do not follow it. Capture is highest on the middle arm (Table 14). Calibration is best on the strongest arm by ECE and worst on the strongest arm on the semantics-free control, where it reports 0.8150.815 confidence at 0.2540.254 accuracy. Order stability is highest on the two arms with the independent-option and commercial designs, which are the middle and the strongest arm, and lowest on the weakest. Without a baseline ordering none of those non-correspondences would be statable, which is why a table this simple earns its own appendix.

The one caveat.

Jev-1.13’s cell runs on 8,7618{,}761 items against Lod-lille’s 888888, and the three arms are not the same size, architecture or license. The condition is matched on the task, not on the models, and a capability ordering across three systems chosen for architectural contrast is not a benchmark ranking. We use it as a reference point internal to this paper and would not quote it as one.

Appendix M Unit integrity

Figure 9 plots the E3 perturbations described in §5.5. The options are byte-identical across all six variants, so the only difference reaching the model is the state string. Table 11 shows the six states for one idiom exactly as they were logged.

Reading Table 11.

The table is the one place in the paper where the actual strings reaching the model are shown, and it is worth reading closely because two of its rows look like typesetting errors and are not. The word shuffle and reversed rows carry the same string: for a three-word expression a particular shuffle and the reversal coincide, and the harness logged both conditions independently and happened to produce the same state. We print what was logged. Equally, the substitute one word row replaces the final word with an unrelated token, producing a string that is not Bengali in any idiomatic sense, and the model’s probability on the gold gloss rises from 0.210.21 to 0.240.24. That single cell is the clearest illustration of §5.5: damaging the expression beyond recognition does not cost the model anything, because the expression was not what it was reading.

The one row that moves is the carrier sentence, and it moves downward here (0.21→0.070.21\rightarrow 0.07) even though context raises accuracy on average by 0.0800.080 and 0.1170.117. A single item is not evidence against the aggregate; we include it rather than hunting for an item that agrees with the mean, because the aggregate is the claim and the item is an illustration.

The lower block shows the E6 forms applied to the gold option. The scrambled row is worth comparing word by word with the full gloss: it contains the same lexical inventory in an order no Bengali reader would accept, and costs the models almost nothing (Table 20). The last row is the semantics-free control, and the table makes concrete what that control removes, which is everything except the option’s label.

What each perturbation is supposed to break.

The six states form a graded attack on the expression’s integrity. Intact is the baseline. Word shuffle destroys word order while preserving the lexical inventory, so a model storing the expression as an ordered unit should fail while a model matching its words should not. Reversed is the specific shuffle that is maximally far from the original in order while being deterministic rather than sampled. Delete one word removes material, which should hurt any model relying on the full form. Substitute one word replaces material with an unrelated token, producing a string that is not the idiom at all and is not idiomatic Bengali. Carrier sentence adds the corpus’s own example sentence around the intact idiom, which adds disambiguating context without touching the expression.

Reading the two panels together.

Accuracy on the left and intact-agreement on the right answer different questions, and either alone is misleading. Accuracy can stay flat because the perturbation does nothing, or because it changes many answers in compensating directions. Agreement distinguishes those: it counts the share of items whose answer is unchanged from the intact state, so a model that is unaffected scores high on both while a model that is churning scores flat accuracy and low agreement. Laya-ml agrees with itself on 0.7420.742 of items under shuffling and Lod-lille on 0.9170.917. For Lod-lille the perturbation is close to invisible. For Laya-ml it is not negligible, but it is no larger than what a meaning-preserving rewrite does: the annotators’ certified alternative forms leave Laya-ml’s answer unchanged on only 0.6570.657 of pairs (Appendix N). Scrambling the expression’s word order moves this model no more than paraphrasing it faithfully, which is the opposite of what a model holding the expression as an ordered unit would show.

What this rules out, and what it does not.

It rules out the hypothesis that these models hold the idiom as a stored lexical unit whose retrieval is keyed on its exact form, because breaking the form does not cost them the answer. It does not establish what they do instead. The state string is read: §5.6 shows a literal gloss that contains the idiom verbatim is chosen more often. What the shuffle shows is that its word order carries little, which fits a model that reads the expression as a set of words. The carrier sentence is the only manipulation that moves either arm, by +0.080+0.080 and +0.117+0.117, and it is the one that adds context rather than altering the expression. Our reading is that the usable figurative signal is in the surrounding material rather than in the expression’s form, and we state it as a reading.

What E3 can and cannot show.

Three scope conditions bound it, and we state them rather than leaving them to be inferred.

The perturbations are real. E3 selects idioms of three words or more under the same tokenizer the distractor builder uses. The corpus holds 1,7911{,}791 such idioms and the logged outputs cover 1,7781{,}778 of them, 1,1361{,}136 of three words, 495495 of four and 147147 longer; the 1313 missing are absent from the logged output rather than excluded by the rule, and at 0.7%0.7\% of the condition they move no reported figure. No manipulation is a no-op on a one- or two-word string. Measured against the logged intact state, the shuffle changes the string on 99.9%99.9\% of items, reversal on 99.7%99.7\%, deletion and substitution on 100%100\%. The one genuine collision is between shuffle and reversal, which coincide on 16.0%16.0\% of items because a three-word reversal is one of only six permutations; we report both rows rather than merging them.

Accuracy is floored. The condition is d-lit, where intact accuracy is already 0.1570.157 and 0.0720.072, below the 0.2500.250 chance level. A perturbation that destroyed the figurative reading entirely could not push accuracy much lower, so the flat accuracy rows are weak evidence on their own and we do not rest the conclusion on them. Agreement with the intact answer has no such floor: it can run from 00 to 11 regardless of how accurate either answer is, and it is 0.7420.742 and 0.9170.917 under shuffling. That is the number the “not a unit” reading rests on. Running E3 under d-rand, where there is headroom above chance, would let accuracy carry the argument too, and we did not.

Power. Lod-lille’s E3 runs on 180180 items, so several of its individual perturbation contrasts are not separately significant and we do not claim them. The claim is the pattern across six conditions and two arms, and the one contrast that is individually large in both.

Appendix N Surface invariance

The corpus ships alternative surface forms certified by annotators as meaning-preserving: a variant spelling, a clipped form, or a near-synonymous rewording recorded in the alternative_idioms field by the same experts who wrote the glosses. These are not perturbations of ours. A model reading meaning rather than form should return the same answer on both members of such a pair. E2 presents each pair under the d-hard family, so the literal gloss is in the option list for both members and the comparison is made under the condition where capture is strongest.

Laya-ml agrees with itself on 0.6570.657 of 3,1433{,}143 pairs (2,4232{,}423 items) and Lod-lille on 0.6770.677 of 310310 pairs (234234 items): about a third of the time, a rewrite the annotators certified as meaning-preserving changes the answer. Mean Jensen–Shannon divergence between the two returned probability vectors is 0.0390.039 and 0.0850.085, on a scale where 00 is identical and 11 is disjoint support.

Reading agreement against divergence.

The two numbers look inconsistent and are not. Small mean divergence with frequent answer changes is the signature of decisions taken on thin margins: the rewrite moves the distribution only slightly, but enough to cross the argmax boundary. Laya-ml’s mean peak probability on these pairs is 0.5350.535, so its top two options are often close and a small shift reorders them (Appendix H gives the full distributions). Lod-lille is the harder case at 0.7370.737: its distributions are sharp, yet it still changes answer on a third of pairs, so for that arm the thin-margin reading covers part of the instability rather than all of it.

Why this is reported as a control rather than a headline.

E2 is the experiment designed to explain the E1 result away, and it does not. If capture were an artifact of the particular surface form the corpus happens to record, presenting the annotators’ alternative form should recover the figurative reading. It does not. Accuracy does move, and significantly: 0.138→0.1930.138\rightarrow 0.193 for Laya-ml and 0.035→0.1580.035\rightarrow 0.158 for Lod-lille (McNemar exact p<0.001p<0.001 on both), so the surface form is not irrelevant. These canonical-form accuracies are lower than the d-hard rows of Table 8 (0.1440.144 and 0.0630.063) because E2 runs only on the items that carry an annotated alternative form, 2,4232{,}423 of 8,8768{,}876 and 234234 of 888888, and that subset is harder for both arms; the comparison here is within the pair, so the level does not affect it. But both forms sit far below the 0.2500.250 chance level on both arms, so the alternative form rescues neither model. We read the two results together: these scorers are genuinely unstable under meaning-preserving rewriting, which is worth reporting on its own, and that instability is neither large enough nor in the right direction to be the mechanism behind a lar of 0.6440.644 to 0.8850.885.

Caveat on the pairs.

Items vary in how many alternative forms they carry, so the pair counts exceed the item counts and items with more variants are weighted more heavily. We report the pair-level figure because it is the quantity a caller experiences; averaging within item first gives 0.6670.667 and 0.6970.697, so the pair weighting lowers agreement by 1.01.0 and 1.91.9 points, which is why the pair-level figure is the more conservative of the two.

Appendix O Subset representativeness

Lod-lille ran a fixed 10%10\% random subset, drawn once with seed 909909 and reused for every experiment on that arm except the capture matrix, which it ran on the full 3,2653{,}265-item pool, so its subset cells are comparable to each other. The question this appendix answers is whether they are comparable to the other arm’s full-set cells. Because the subset is a subset of the same corpus, we can measure the answer directly rather than assume it: Table 19 runs Laya-ml, which has the full set, on those same 888888 items and compares it with itself.

Why this is the right test.

An alternative would be to compare Lod-lille on the subset against Laya-ml on the full set and attribute any difference to sampling, which conflates the sample with the model. Holding the model fixed and varying only the sample isolates the sampling term. The drift in Table 19 measures how well the subset stands in for the full corpus. It does not enter the paired cross-arm comparisons, which are made on the shared 888 items where both arms see the same subset.

What the drift column shows.

The largest absolute drift across five families is 0.0160.016, on d-rand. Three families drift down and two up, but the two upward drifts are negligible (+0.001+0.001, +0.004+0.004), so the fair summary is a slight downward lean of under two points rather than no lean at all. Two of the five subset estimates fall marginally outside the full-set bootstrap interval, which at n=888n=888 against n=8,876n=8{,}876 is the expected rate rather than a signal. Critically, no family’s drift is large enough to reorder the ladder: d-lit and d-hard remain far below the other three on both the full set and the subset, and the d-rand to d-lit gap, which is the quantity the paper reports, changes by 0.0010.001.

Appendix P Full option ablation

Table 20 gives the numbers behind Figure 10. The five rows hold the state, the instruction and the gold position fixed and rewrite every option in the list the same way, so a row is a statement about what the option text needs to contain for the decision to survive.

The first three rows are the finding.

Truncating each option to its first six words costs 0.0040.004, 0.0240.024 and 0.0110.011 across the three arms. Scrambling the words inside each option, which leaves a string no reader of either language would accept as a sentence, costs 0.0080.008, 0.0130.013 and nothing at all; on Jev-1.13 the scrambled row is marginally above the full gloss, which is within noise but makes the point that the manipulation is invisible to it. Taken together: what these models need from an option is its lexical inventory, and the order and syntax of that inventory are close to free. This is the behavioral half of the result Sun et al. (2026) reach from the other direction by permuting which option name is bound to which definition.

The fourth row is a separate effect.

Presenting the options in the other language, with the state unchanged, costs Laya-ml 0.0180.018 and Jev-1.13 0.0070.007 but Lod-lille 0.0950.095, which is five to thirteen times as much. The arm that loses most from a language mismatch between state and options is the arm whose documentation reports English-only training evaluation, and the one with the largest cross-lingual gap in E4. We note the correspondence; with three models we cannot test it.

The fifth row is the control, and it is the row that validates the instrument.

Replacing every option with a bare label leaves 0.2560.256, 0.2330.233 and 0.2540.254, against a chance level of 0.2500.250. This matters more than it looks. It shows that the four preceding rows are measuring option semantics rather than some artifact of the harness, because when the semantics are removed the measurement collapses to exactly where it should. It also shows the gold-position randomization is working: a harness with a position leak would score above chance here. And it is the condition §5.3 builds on, because it is the one place where accuracy is known a priori, at 0.250.25, so any reported confidence above that is unambiguously excess.

Caveats.

Three bound what the o-series shows. First, truncation to six words is a weaker manipulation than it sounds: the median Bengali gloss is four words, so truncation leaves 77.8%77.8\% of options untouched, and the English options, median seven words, are cut on 58.0%58.0\%. The scramble is the informative row: it is necessarily a no-op on the 5.7%5.7\% of options that are a single word, and otherwise changes the option’s word order. Second, the whole series runs on random distractors, where identifying the right words already suffices to answer; a model that composes meaning and one that only matches words would both score well. So these rows show that composition is not required on this condition, not that these models cannot compose. Running the scramble under d-lit or d-sem, where the distractors are lexically close and composition would pay, is the test that would separate the two, and we did not run it. Third, Jev-1.13’s column is English throughout, so its rows are not comparable in level to the other two, only in shape. The three arms’ full gloss rows differ slightly from the corresponding d-rand rows of Table 8 because E6 draws its own distractor sample, under seed 60006000 on the open arms and 1600016000 on the commercial arm, whose E6 also runs on 873873 items rather than 3,2653{,}265; the differences are 0.0020.002 to 0.0080.008 and we report both rather than reconciling them silently.

Appendix Q Order sensitivity and position bias

This appendix reports the per-slot selection shares behind §5.4, then sets out the permutation audit that establishes the residual instability of the independent-option scorer is real rather than an artifact of our harness.

What is held fixed.

Each item here is one idiom with one fixed set of four option texts. We present that same set 24 times, once per permutation, and change nothing else: the instruction string, the state, kk, the decoding configuration and the option texts themselves are byte-identical across the 24 calls, and no call is retried. The only quantity that varies is which slot, and therefore which letter, each option occupies. Anything that moves across the 24 calls is attributable to that reordering, which cannot separate position from labeling (§5.4): the condition is clean in what it holds fixed, not in what it can attribute.

Item samples.

The three arms’ item samples were drawn separately, 992992 for Laya-ml, 299299 for Lod-lille and 300300 for Jev-1.13, and barely overlap: no item is common to all three, and any two share at most 3333. Every cross-arm figure in Tables 21 and 22 is therefore a comparison of rates on different items, not a paired one. At these sizes the gap between 83.7%83.7\% and 10.7%10.7\% is far outside sampling error, but item composition is not controlled across arms.

Recovering option identity.

The harness records, per call, the permutation as a four-digit string in which position ss holds the index, in the canonical option list, of the option displayed in slot ss. A chosen slot must be mapped back through that permutation before it can be compared across calls. Counting distinct slot letters instead inflates instability to near unity for any scorer, because a letter necessarily changes whenever the same gloss is moved; on Laya-ml that metric reads 1.0001.000 against the 0.8370.837 reported here. It is an easy substitution to make and it is not what we want to measure, so we flag it. All numbers in the paper use the mapped gloss identity.

The permutation audit.

Table 22 reports a quantity that the summary measures in Table 21 cannot: not whether the answer changes, but how far a single option’s own score travels as that option is moved around the list. This is the quantity the independent-option design makes a claim about. Scoring every option from the same start position, so that no option attends to any other, should make an option’s score a function of that option and the state alone, so the spread should sit at the level of floating-point accumulation noise, which for fp32 summation over sequences of this length is on the order of 10−710^{-7}. It does not. Lod-lille’s median item has an option whose score moves 4.0×10−24.0\times 10^{-2}, five orders of magnitude higher, and not one of its 299 items falls below 10−410^{-4}. Two consequences follow. First, the 10.7%10.7\% answer-change rate in Table 21 is not a tie-breaking or slot-indexing artifact of our harness: ties would require near-identical scores, and the scores are not near-identical, so what moves is the scoring itself. Second, the documented guarantee is not one an evaluation can rely on, at least in the configuration we were able to run. We take the narrow reading throughout: the independent-option design is a large improvement over the marker-based one on this axis, and it is not the categorical property its documentation describes.

The commercial arm.

Jev-1.13 makes no public invariance claim, and its behavior is the least like either open arm. It returns identical distributions on 23.0%23.0\% of items, with the caveat above that its probabilities reach us rounded to two decimal places, so this describes the reported values rather than the computation behind them. Against that, its mean spread (0.1390.139) is three times Lod-lille’s and its maximum (0.8200.820) approaches Laya-ml’s. The distribution is bimodal rather than merely noisier, which is what one would expect from a scorer that is close to deterministic on easy items and switches regime on hard ones. We cannot test that reading without weights, and we do not claim it.

Position bias.

Figure 12 gives the distributional summaries behind Table 21, both from the permutation sweep. Figure 11 is the one panel in this appendix drawn from a different run: it reports per-slot selection shares over the full ladder condition, pooled over its families, on 8,8768{,}876 items for Laya-ml, 888888 for Lod-lille and 8,7618{,}761 for Jev-1.13, because position is randomized per item there and the estimate is far better powered than the sweep’s 992992 items would allow. The sweep agrees in direction and is milder, 32.7%32.7\% against 18.8%18.8\% on slot B and slot A for Laya-ml. Because the gold option is placed uniformly at random in both, the expectation under no positional bias is exactly 0.250.25 in every slot for every arm, so neither needs a baseline model: the distance from the dashed line is the bias. Laya-ml’s profile is not the primacy gradient usually reported for prompted generative scorers (Zheng et al., 2024); it peaks on slot B at 37.2%37.2\% against 14.6%14.6\% for slot A, a 2.5×2.5\times swing in selection share from position alone, and is not a monotone function of position at all. We note the shape and decline to explain it; with one model per scoring design, we have no way to separate a property of the marker scheme from a property of this particular backbone.

Appendix R Run record

Environment.

Python 3.13.15 throughout. The two open arms ran on one Tesla T4 (15,360 MiB): Laya-ml with amp_dtype set to bf16 and max_len 1024 at 27.2 ms per call, Lod-lille in fp32 at 86.1 ms per call. The T4 is Turing, whose tensor cores take fp16 and integer inputs only, so there is no native bf16 path and no fp32 or tf32 tensor-core path either: the autocast context accepts the setting and the arithmetic falls back to ordinary fp32 CUDA cores, with bf16 rounding only at the cast boundaries. We report the configured value because that is what the run record holds, and flag it because a reader comparing against an Ampere or later card is not comparing the same numerics.

The commercial arm needs no accelerator and ran on CPU against typesafe/jev-1.13. That alias is mutable: at the time of our run it resolved to the 20260917 build, and a later caller using the same alias may not reach the same weights. Every commercial figure in this paper should be read against that build.

Release.

The instrument, the per-item outputs for every cell, the analysis scripts and the figure sources are available under CC BY-SA 4.0 at https://github.com/sakhadib/literal-lock-in, with the project page at https://sakhadib.github.io/literal-lock-in.

Temperatures.

Laya-ml’s run recorded temperature = [1.0, 1.0, 1.0] with temperature_by_options empty, so the per-bucket temperatures it ships were not applied and its ECE figures are raw. Lod-lille ships temperature: 1.0 by design, its authors having reported that fitting hurt held-out calibration. Both open arms are therefore untempered and comparable on that axis. The commercial arm’s internal calibration is not observable.

Seeds.

The Bengali arms use a per-experiment seed (E1 1000, E2 2000, E3 3000, E4 4000, E6 6000, E7 7000) added to the item id, so each item’s option permutation is reproducible and identical across arms. The split seed is 20261001. The commercial arm uses a disjoint block seed set (order audit 17000, literal 12000, ceiling 11000, Bengali control 14000, options 16000) because its blocks ran in a different order; the permutation for a given item is still a pure function of seed and id. Lod-lille’s 10% subset was drawn once with seed 909909.

Call volume and cost.

The commercial arm issued 56,533 calls for $0.9348 at $0.042 per million input tokens with output free. The blocks are the order audit (300300 items × 24\times\,24 permutations =7,200=7{,}200), literal capture on the shared pool (3,265×33{,}265\times 3 families, d-rand, d-lit and d-hard, =9,795=9{,}795), the English ceiling (8,761×38{,}761\times 3 families, d-rand, d-surf and d-sem, =26,283=26{,}283), the Bengali control (8,7618{,}761, one family) and the option ablation (873×5873\times 5 option forms =4,365=4{,}365), which is 56,404 retained rows. The option ablation runs on 873873 items rather than the 888888 of the shared subset because this block is English and 1515 of the 888888 carry no English equivalent idiom to use as the state; the 873873 are exactly the intersection of the subset with the 8,7618{,}761 items that do. The remaining 129 calls are the endpoint probe and the response-contract checks made before each block. Transient 429 and 5xx responses were retried with exponential backoff to a 30 s ceiling; no call was dropped.

Statistics.

All intervals are 95% percentile bootstrap over items, 2,000 resamples, fixed seed 0. ECE uses 15 equal-width bins. Paired comparisons use McNemar’s exact test via the binomial distribution. AURC is reported against a random-gate baseline computed on the same items. Differences and ratios are computed from unrounded values, so they can differ in the last digit from differences of the printed figures.

What is released.

The per-item outputs for every cell of every experiment (one row per item per condition, carrying the full probability vector, the predicted key, the gold key, the literal key and the gold position), the five split manifests, the three run environment records quoted above, the task configurations containing the verbatim instruction strings, the analysis scripts that turn those outputs into every table in this paper, the figure sources, and, beside each figure, a CSV of the exact plotted values.

Pairing.

Because the two open arms were reconstructed independently from a written contract rather than from shared code, the released outputs admit a direct check: on the 4,440 overlapping rows the gold key, gold position, idiom string and literal-distractor key agree at 1.0001.000. That check is itself a released artifact, and it is what licenses every paired test in the paper.

The matrix run.

The six cells of §5.1 were run as one job, with their own seed namespace (21000) so no option permutation collides with the runs above. Every cell covers the same 3,265 items and is built by a single function; the two languages share one distractor draw per item and are shuffled independently from the same generator. Laya-ml ran both languages on the multilingual checkpoint, so only the language changes and the checkpoint does not. Lod-lille ran the full pool here rather than its 10% subset, so its matrix cells rest on 3,2653{,}265 items. The commercial arm issued 6,531 calls for $0.1152. Its English cell reproduces its English-ladder value to four decimal places (0.04720.0472), which is the check that the two constructions measure the same thing.

Known gaps.

E2 was not run on the commercial arm, a gap in coverage rather than a constraint of language or cost. Cost was not the constraint: the whole commercial arm came to $1.05, the $0.9348 of the main blocks plus the $0.1152 of the matrix run. The matrix covers the literal condition only; the other distractor families were not run in both languages. The confidence inversion remains a two-arm result, although §5.2 reports the commercial arm’s Bengali calibration from the matrix outputs.
